summary: A paper proposing a scheme, called ENCAPS, which the author believes is a good medium-term solution to Internet routing and addressing problems, tied to the IPng effort. It is informational.

eli5.summary: One person's idea for fixing how the Internet finds addresses and routes, shared as a suggestion for others to consider.

questions: proposals for internet routing and addressing in the 1990s
subtitle: A medium-term routing scheme using IP header encapsulation for autonomous domains

tldr.problem: The Internet faced growing routing table size in the early 1990s as the number of networks increased, but the IETF had not yet agreed on a long-term solution like IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: ENCAPS proposes that border routers encapsulate IP datagrams with an outer IP header that routes by autonomous domain (AD) rather than individual network. Interior routers never see the outer header, keeping their routing tables small while preserving the current IP addressing scheme.
tldr.outcome: This was one of several medium-term proposals circulated during the IPng debates, but IPv6 and later BGP improvements ultimately solved the scaling problem differently.
tldr.outcomeLabel: A proposal that did not prevail

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Not adopted; largely superseded by IPv6 and BGP improvements

today: RFC 1955 is an Informational RFC representing one proposal in the mid-1990s IPng debates. The ENCAPS approach was not adopted; instead, the Internet ultimately deployed IPv6 for long-term addressing and refined BGP for routing scalability. The RFC remains historically interesting as a window into the routing challenges and proposed solutions of that era.

sections.title: The Routing Scale Problem
sections.content:
RFC 1955 proposes ENCAPS, a medium-term solution to Internet routing and addressing problems. In 1996, the ROAD (Routing and Addressing) group was working on long-term solutions but had not reached consensus. The RFC notes that the Internet needed a solution that would 'buy time' to develop and deploy a long-term approach, while making only minimal changes to the existing network.

The core issue was that routing tables in backbone routers were growing too large, and the existing IP addressing structure, while still globally unique, could not support indefinitely expanding networks without scalability problems.
sections.eli5: When the internet grew, routers had to remember more and more paths. This idea was a way to group networks temporarily, like putting addresses into neighborhoods, to keep the lists manageable.

sections.title: The ENCAPS Design
sections.content:
The key mechanism is that border routers encapsulate datagrams with an outer IP header that routes by autonomous domain rather than by individual network. When a border router sees a packet destined outside its domain, it adds an outer IP header with the AD (autonomous domain) addresses of the source and destination ADs, then forwards it.

Interior routers inside transit autonomous domains simply forward the encapsulated datagram using the AD addresses, without knowing anything special about it. Only the entrance (first) and exit (last) border routers do the encapsulation and de-encapsulation work. AD addresses are standard IP addresses reserved from a small number of Class A and Class B networks, allowing for millions of autonomous domains.
sections.eli5: Border routers wrap each outgoing message in an extra label saying which neighborhood (AD) it comes from and where it's going. Inside neighborhoods, routers just pass it along. The destination neighborhood unwraps it and hands it to the final address.

sections.title: Stated Advantages
sections.content:
The RFC lists several advantages of ENCAPS:

  • Only border routers and DNS need to change; hosts and interior routers are unaffected
  • No new routing protocols or internet protocols are required
  • No address translation in packets
  • Uses the current IP addressing structure
  • Scales well by organizing domains into commonwealths, so border routers need only know details of their own commonwealth
  • Reduces routing load on all routers and solves the routing table size problem for the foreseeable future

The scheme does impose size limits and does not support new internet services such as guaranteed bandwidth or delay guarantees. It also requires additional processing at border routers.
sections.eli5: Few things need to change: just the border guards and the phone book. Neighborhoods can organize into larger regions, so each border only remembers nearby paths.

sections.title: Historical Context
sections.content:
RFC 1955 was submitted to the IETF IPng area as one of several medium-term proposals during the routing and addressing debates of the mid-1990s. The RFC explicitly states that publication does not imply acceptance by the IPng area of the ideas expressed. It was an open proposal for discussion rather than a consensus recommendation.

Other long-term solutions discussed in that era included CLNP, NAT, IDPR, IDRP, Nimrod, Unified, and NewIP. Ultimately, IPv6 and improvements to inter-domain routing protocols like BGP became the paths forward rather than encapsulation-based schemes.
sections.eli5: This was one person's idea offered during a big debate about the internet's future. Others had different ideas, and eventually the community chose different solutions.

references.text: Gross, P., and P. Almquist, "IESG Deliberations on Routing and Addressing", RFC 1380, ANS, Stanford University, November 1992.
